presentingComplaint: Brought to the emergency department by family after a witnessed generalized seizure at home; noted to be shaking, sweating, and confused for the preceding day.
history: 47-year-old man with a 20-year history of heavy daily alcohol use (approximately 12-15 standard drinks/day) who stopped drinking abruptly 60 hours ago after running out of money and being unable to obtain alcohol. Over the last 36 hours he developed progressively worsening hand tremor, anxiety, insomnia, and profuse sweating. This morning family noted him talking to people who were not present and picking at his clothes. Approximately 2 hours prior to arrival he had a single witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting under 2 minutes with a brief post-ictal period, prompting the ED visit. No prior history of unprovoked seizures. One prior hospitalization for alcohol withdrawal seizures 3 years ago; no prior diagnosed delirium tremens. No reported head trauma, fever prior to today, focal weakness, or recent illicit drug use. No history of liver disease diagnosed but has never had a formal medical evaluation in over a decade.
examination: Agitated, diaphoretic, disoriented to time and place, intermittently picking at the air (visual hallucinations). Coarse bilateral hand tremor at rest, worsened with intention. Marked diaphoresis, flushed skin. No nuchal rigidity. No focal neurological deficits; pupils equal and reactive. Cardiovascular exam: tachycardic, regular rhythm, no murmurs. Abdomen soft, mild hepatomegaly, no ascites or asterixis noted. Tongue bite mark noted on the lateral tongue. No signs of head injury. Gait unsteady but no dysmetria; formal ataxia difficult to assess given agitation.
imaging: Non-contrast CT head: no acute intracranial hemorrhage, mass, or midline shift
microbiology: Blood cultures pending (drawn given low-grade fever, results not yet available)
finalDiagnosis: Delirium tremens (severe alcohol withdrawal syndrome with withdrawal seizure)
citations: Harrison 22e — Alcohol Use Disorder and Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome
American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management 2020
contraindications: Avoid antipsychotics as monotherapy for withdrawal seizures/DTs (lower seizure threshold, do not treat autonomic instability)
Avoid unopposed dextrose administration before thiamine (risk of precipitating/worsening Wernicke encephalopathy)
Avoid physical restraints without adequate sedation (worsens agitation, risk of rhabdomyolysis/hyperthermia)
Use caution with beta-blockers/clonidine as monotherapy — they mask autonomic signs without preventing seizures or delirium; not a substitute for benzodiazepines
edgeCases: This diagnosis (delirium tremens / alcohol withdrawal) is not present in the provided diagnosable-disease list, so acceptableIds is intentionally set to [] and differentialIds only captures indirectly related listed conditions used for differentiation, not the primary diagnosis itself

Wernicke encephalopathy must always be actively excluded/treated empirically in any alcohol-withdrawal patient with confusion, given diagnostic triad (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia) is frequently incomplete
Fever and tachycardia in DTS can mimic sepsis; concurrent infection must be excluded but should not delay withdrawal-directed treatment
Hypomagnesemia and hypokalemia are common and can independently lower seizure threshold and worsen arrhythmia risk
Single withdrawal seizure does not mandate long-term antiepileptic therapy; management is benzodiazepine-based, not phenytoin
expectedMaiK: MaiK should flag this as severe alcohol withdrawal/delirium tremens with a recent withdrawal seizure, prioritizing front-loaded benzodiazepine therapy (symptom-triggered or fixed-schedule per CIWA-Ar), empiric thiamine before glucose, and correction of magnesium/potassium/phosphate, while excluding Wernicke encephalopathy, sepsis/CNS infection, and structural brain lesions as mimics.
expectedNextQuestions: What is the time since last alcohol intake and quantity/pattern of use?
Is there a prior history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens?
Has thiamine been given before any glucose-containing fluids?
What is the CIWA-Ar score and trend?
Are there any focal neurological findings or signs of head trauma requiring neuroimaging?
Is there evidence of infection (fever source workup) or aspiration risk given agitation?
What are the current electrolyte levels, especially magnesium, potassium, and phosphate?
Is there any co-ingestion (benzodiazepines, opioids, illicit stimulants) that could alter management?
